and an analysis from an educated user below:



Nota · Yuki MCP (ctxlayer)
Hoe Claude aan ctxlayer hangt, en waar het stil breekt
Aan Steven
Van Jan Peeters
Datum 17 sep 2026
Aanleiding: meerdere collega's melden dat ze Yuki MCP in Claude dagelijks opnieuw moeten verbinden — iets wat tot voor kort niet nodig was. Zelf zie ik iets anders: alles toont “verbonden”, maar een dienst werkt pas weer na opnieuw autoriseren in ctxlayer — en in de tussentijd is er geen melding, zodat het model antwoorden kan verzinnen. Dat zijn twee verschillende dingen.

Deel 1 legt uit hoe Claude met ctxlayer verbindt — het verschil tussen de “connector” in de chat-app en de MCP-setup in Claude Code — omdat daar veel van de meldingen uit voortkomen. Deel 2 beschrijft het eigenlijke probleem: de diensten achter ctxlayer verliezen hun autorisatie zonder enige melding of zichtbaar signaal. Alles wat als gemeten staat is op 17 september vastgesteld in Claude Code.

Deel 1
Connector versus MCP-setup: hoe Claude met ctxlayer verbindt
ctxlayer is één remote MCP-server op één adres, https://mcp.yukitools.dev/mcp, met OAuth 2.1 (Dynamic Client Registration + PKCE). De setup-pagina noemt drie manieren om die server aan een Claude-client te hangen: in Claude Code met claude mcp add --transport http ctxlayer … gevolgd door /mcp → Authenticate; in Claude Desktop en de web-app via Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector; en in editors via hun eigen mcp.json. ctxlayer zelf kent geen “connector”: dat is alleen het woord van de chat-app voor een toegevoegde remote MCP-server. Voor de gateway zijn het allemaal OAuth-clients op hetzelfde adres.

Connector
via het Claude-account: chat, Cowork én Code
Lokale MCP-registratie
claude mcp add — alleen Code op die machine
eigen login
per client
ctxlayer
gateway
autorisatie
per dienst, per gebruiker
Linear · ADO · Sentry
Datadog · GitHub · Notion · …
Links: twee routes, elk met een eigen login op dezelfde gateway. Rechts: jouw autorisaties per dienst, die voor beide routes gelden (daarover gaat deel 2).
Twee routes, twee logins
Er zijn twee manieren om ctxlayer aan Claude te hangen, en elk heeft een eigen login-token. De connector hangt aan je Claude-account en geldt daardoor overal waar je met dat account werkt: de chat-app, Cowork én Claude Code. De lokale registratie via claude mcp add hangt aan Claude Code op die machine en geldt alleen daar. Het token van de ene route is niet bruikbaar voor de andere.

Connector
hangt aan het Claude-account
Hoe toegevoegd
Settings → Connectors → “Yuki MCP” → Connect
Wie zette het klaar
De org: staat al in de workspace als “installed for Yuki BE”. Inloggen blijft per gebruiker.
Login-token
Eigen token, aan het account
Geldt voor
Chat-app, Cowork én Claude Code
Mijn situatie gemeten
Nooit ingelogd: status “Not connected”, geen tools in chat of Cowork
Lokale registratie
hangt aan Claude Code op die machine
Hoe toegevoegd
claude mcp add …, daarna /mcp → Authenticate
Wie zette het klaar
De gebruiker zelf
Login-token
Eigen token, lokaal bij Claude Code
Geldt voor
Alleen Claude Code op die machine
Mijn situatie gemeten
Ingelogd en verbonden; hierdoor werkt Code bij mij
Daarom kan Code bij mij werken terwijl de connector “Not connected” toont: Code draait op de lokale registratie, en op de connector is gewoon nog nooit ingelogd. Dat is geen storing. Eén keer Connect en de connector werkt in chat, Cowork én Code. De autorisaties voor Linear, ADO en Sentry hoeven daarna niet opnieuw — die hangen aan de gebruiker, niet aan de route. Wie beide routes heeft, ziet ctxlayer in Code twee keer staan; één route is genoeg.

Wat er met de login-token gebeurt
De login op de gateway levert een kortlopend access-token en een refresh-token. De client vernieuwt het access-token stil; normaal merk je daar niets van. Faalt dat vernieuwen, dan valt die ene route eruit en moet je voor die route opnieuw inloggen.

gemeten  Mijn Code-login op 17-09: access-token en refresh-token beide aanwezig; het access-token verliep binnen het uur en werd stil vernieuwd; de verbinding hield de hele sessie. Bij een gezonde login is er dus geen dagelijkse herverbinding.

Dit is nieuw. Tot voor kort bleef de verbinding gewoon staan; de dagelijkse herverbinding begon pas recent, en je gaf zelf aan dat je in die periode wijzigingen aan de gateway hebt gedaan. Dat is de meest waarschijnlijke oorzaak: iets in die wijziging heeft bestaande refresh-tokens of client-registraties ongeldig gemaakt, zodat het stil vernieuwen faalt en clients er telkens uitvallen. Vanaf de client is niet te zien wát precies — de OAuth-app, scopes, sleutels, de levensduur of rotatie van refresh-tokens, of het bewaren van client-registraties.

Eén voorbehoud bij het triëren van zulke meldingen: een connector waarop nooit is ingelogd toont óók “Not connected”, maar dat is geen uitval. Eerste vraag blijft dus: via de connector, of via claude mcp add?

Vraag aan jou
Welke wijziging is er precies gedaan, en raakt die de refresh-tokens of de client-registraties van bestaande logins?
Bevestigen de logs van mislukte refresh-pogingen per client sinds die wijziging dat beeld?
Uitrol
Connector: staat al klaar in de workspace; per gebruiker één keer Connect in Settings → Connectors, en chat, Cowork én Code werken.
Lokale registratie: alternatief voor wie ctxlayer alleen in Claude Code wil — per gebruiker claude mcp add …, of een .mcp.json in de repo zodat iedereen die daarin werkt het erbij krijgt en zijn eigen MCP-servers houdt.
Deel 2
Het probleem: diensten achter ctxlayer verliezen hun autorisatie zonder luide melding of zichtbare disconnect
Achter de gateway hangen de diensten. Voor elk daarvan geef je ctxlayer één keer toestemming op /app/upstreams. Zo'n autorisatie is per gebruiker, geldt voor al je clients tegelijk, en heeft haar eigen looptijd bij die dienst — los van je login op de gateway en los van de andere diensten. Het geldt voor de diensten met een persoonlijke autorisatie: ADO, Datadog, GitHub, Linear, Notion, Sentry, Survicate en Yuki IA NL. Driver, Tokenspend en Yuki PDD Org draaien op een gedeeld token en hebben dit probleem niet. Of dit nieuw is, weet ik niet.

Wat er misgaat gemeten
Een autorisatie verloopt, en nergens wordt dat zichtbaar. De Upstreams-pagina en list_upstreams blijven “verbonden” tonen. Bij de start van mijn sessie op 17-09:

up-linear     connected: true    needsReauth: true    toolsCount: 0
              note: "credential refresh failed — this session registered none of its tools;
                     reconnect the upstream at /app/upstreams, then call reload_upstreams"
up-survicate  connected: false                        toolsCount: 18
alle andere   connected: true   — en gaven op een echte call ook echte data terug
Linear stond tegelijk op verbonden én op “opnieuw autoriseren”, met nul bruikbare tools. Survicate was niet verbonden maar telde toch 18 tools. De status komt dus niet uit een echte controle van de autorisatie. De Upstreams-pagina in de UI toont hetzelfde beeld en is daarmee evenmin te vertrouwen als gezondheidssignaal.

Twee uitkomsten voor de gebruiker
Zichtbaar. De gateway registreert nul tools voor die dienst; een call is onmogelijk en de agent merkt het. Vervelend, maar veilig. Dit was Linear op 17-09 — en alleen omdat de foutmelding letterlijk in het antwoord stond, kon een lokale controle erop aanslaan.
Onzichtbaar. Alles staat op verbonden, de tools zijn er, maar een call komt leeg of fout terug zonder foutmelding — en het model behandelt dat als een echt antwoord en verzint. Dit is wat ik eerder deze week meemaakte en wat meerdere gebruikers melden. Op 17-09 niet gereproduceerd: alle fouten waren die dag zichtbaar. Dit is het gevaarlijke geval.
Herstel geeft evenmin een signaal gemeten
Na opnieuw autoriseren van Linear op /app/upstreams:

reload_upstreams  →  added: []   "Nothing new: no upstream connected since this
                                    session started and every catalogued tool is
                                    already registered."
list_upstreams    →  up-linear  connected: true   toolsCount: 79   (needsReauth weg)
De dienst ging van 0 naar 79 tools, maar reload_upstreams meldde dat er niets veranderd was. De tools kwamen pas later in de sessie beschikbaar, zonder dat daar een melding van kwam. Een gebruiker kan de werkelijke toestand dus alleen vaststellen door zelf per dienst een echte call te doen.

Waarom dit erger is dan een verloren login. Bij een verloren login (deel 1) zie je dat de verbinding weg is en log je opnieuw in. Hier zie je niets: de status blijft groen, er is geen melding bij verlopen, geen melding bij herstel, en het antwoord kan fout zijn. Wat nodig is, is precies wat nu ontbreekt: luid melden en zichtbaar disconnecten in ctxlayer zodra een autorisatie wegvalt.

Vragen aan jou
Luid melden: kan ctxlayer de gebruiker een duidelijke notificatie geven zodra een autorisatie verloopt of een refresh faalt — in plaats van dat je het ontdekt aan een fout antwoord?
Zichtbaar disconnecten: kan de Upstreams-pagina en list_upstreams die dienst dan ook echt als niet verbonden tonen, met een status uit een echte controle in plaats van uit cache — zodat connected en needsReauth nooit tegelijk waar zijn?
Kan een call op een verlopen autorisatie altijd een harde fout teruggeven — nooit een leeg of gedeeltelijk “succes”?
Kan reload_upstreams rapporteren wat er werkelijk veranderde, zodat ook herstel zichtbaar is?

# ctxlayer-ops (private)

Hosting/operations for the **ctxlayer.net** managed service. Kept out of the
open-source app repo on purpose — this holds the multi-tenant provisioning,
the per-host wrangler template, the tenant registry, generated secrets, and
the marketing-site deploy.

The application itself is the separate open-source repo (`../ctxlayer` by
default; override with `APP_REPO=/path/to/ctxlayer`). Scenario **B** — one
isolated Cloudflare Worker deployment per tenant/env, **zero app-code
changes**. See the app repo's `docs/plan/K-multitenancy.md` for the design.

## Layout

```
wrangler.template.toml      per-host config template (envsubst → wrangler.<slug>.toml in the app repo)
scripts/provision-tenant.sh stand up one host (resources + secrets + migrate + deploy + register)
scripts/release-all.sh      re-render + migrate + deploy across hosts (the ONLY upgrade path)
scripts/deprovision-tenant.sh  tear a host down
scripts/deploy-marketing.sh deploy the static marketing site to Cloudflare Pages
tenants.json                registry: slug → {d1, kv, host}   (gitignored)
.tenant-secrets/<slug>.env  generated ENCRYPTION_KEY/SESSION_COOKIE_SECRET (gitignored — move to a real store)
```

## Prerequisites

- `wrangler` logged into the Cloudflare account that owns the `ctxlayer.net` zone.
- `bun`, `jq`, `envsubst` (gettext), `openssl`, `curl`.
- The app repo checked out as a sibling (`../ctxlayer`) or `APP_REPO` set.

## Conventions

- **Hosts:** `<slug>.ctxlayer.net`. dev/test = `dev`, staging = `stage`.
- **Reserved (non-tenant) labels:** `www docs support dev api stage`.
  `www` is the marketing site; `docs/support/api` are placeholders; `dev`/`stage`
  are our own envs (provision with `--infra`).
- **Sign-in:** one GitHub OAuth App per host (callback
  `https://<host>/idp/github/callback`) — create by hand, pass id/secret.
- **No auto-upgrade:** hosts only move when you run `release-all.sh`; each
  advertises its running commit in the SPA footer + `GET /api/health`.

## Recipes

```bash
# stand up the non-prod envs (each needs its own GitHub OAuth App):
GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=… GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=… scripts/provision-tenant.sh dev   admin@you  --infra
GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=… GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=… scripts/provision-tenant.sh stage admin@you  --infra

# stand up a tenant:
GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=… GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=… scripts/provision-tenant.sh acme  admin@acme

# ship the current app checkout everywhere (or to named hosts):
scripts/release-all.sh
scripts/release-all.sh dev stage

# marketing site (Cloudflare Pages, served at www.ctxlayer.net):
MARKETING_DIR="/Users/stevenn/Claude/Projects/ctxlayer Marketing" scripts/deploy-marketing.sh
```

## Marketing site notes

`deploy-marketing.sh` deploys a **staged copy** of the site that physically
omits `INTERNAL-NOTES.md` (pricing), `README.md`, `.gitignore`, `.assetsignore`.
Cloudflare Pages does **not** honour `.assetsignore` on `wrangler pages deploy`
(verified — the first unstaged deploy leaked the pricing file), so do not rely
on it. One-time: add `www.ctxlayer.net` as a Pages custom domain and a zone
Redirect Rule `ctxlayer.net` → `https://www.ctxlayer.net` (301).

# Plan — `mcp.yukitools.dev` (Phase 6: MCP endpoint behind Entra)

Status: **LIVE — deployed & verified 2026-06-25.** Companion to `yukitools-sso-runbook.md`.
The browser app (`ctxlayer.yukitools.dev`) is live behind Access; the **MCP** surface at
`mcp.yukitools.dev` is now live for Entra/Yuki users. See **Implementation status** at the bottom.

## Mental model (read this first)

The OAuth flow is **already built into ctxlayer** — `@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider`
gives us the whole MCP Authorization Server: dynamic client registration
(`/oauth/register`), `/oauth/authorize`, `/oauth/token`,
`/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`, the bearer-gated `/mcp` transport, and
grant completion (`completeMcpAuthorization`). **We are not building an OAuth server.**

This phase is **~90% mounting + ~10% one identity bridge**:
- **Mounting:** serve the app on `mcp.yukitools.dev`, keep the machine endpoints
  public, gate only `/oauth/authorize` behind Access.
- **Bridge:** the built-in `/oauth/authorize` logs the human in via the app's own
  GitHub/Google chooser. Yuki users are **Entra** (no GitHub org / Google Workspace),
  so they can't complete it. We add **one login option** to that existing step:
  trust the Cloudflare Access JWT (Entra-via-Access). Reuses the verifier we already
  shipped. *(If MCP users could use GitHub/Google, this phase would be 100% mounting,
  zero code.)*

Cloudflare Access is the **IdP feeding identity into our OAuth server**, not the
OAuth server itself (it has no DCR / MCP discovery).

## Decision: **Option A** — reuse the Access-JWT trust on `/oauth/authorize`

One Worker, a 2nd custom domain. Minimal code, reuses everything, no new env vars,
same database as the browser app. (Option B — a generic OIDC IdP provider pointed at
Access-for-SaaS OIDC — is a larger, ~6–10h change; nice open-source addition later,
not needed for Yuki's internal MCP. See bottom.)

### Key facts that make this clean (verified 2026-06-24)
- **OAuth layer is request-host-relative.** `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` is **not** passed to the
  OAuthProvider (`oauth/provider-config.ts` only sets endpoint paths). The library
  derives issuer/metadata/token-`aud` from the **request Host**. So a 2nd custom domain
  on the same Worker advertises `mcp.yukitools.dev/oauth/*` and issues host-correct
  tokens. `PUBLIC_BASE_URL` stays `ctxlayer.yukitools.dev` (only drives the browser
  app's IdP callbacks + CSRF, which Option A doesn't touch).
- **Same-origin OAuth is preserved** — all OAuth endpoints stay on `mcp.yukitools.dev`;
  we gate only the `/oauth/authorize` *path*, not a separate host.
- **MCP transport is bearer-only** (`mcp/session-do.ts` reads `this.props`; no cookies,
  no Access header). So `/mcp`, `/oauth/token`, `/oauth/register`, `/.well-known/*` are
  safe to expose publicly — they're secured by the bearer + DCR.
- **Migration `0028` already allows `idp='access'`**, and `CF_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN` +
  `CF_ACCESS_AUD` are already set on the Worker. No new env, no schema change.

## Topology

```
Worker ctxlayer-yukitools (one deployment, one DB)
├── ctxlayer.yukitools.dev      → host-level Access app (browser SPA, gated)  ✅ live
└── mcp.yukitools.dev           → 2nd custom domain, PUBLIC by default
       /.well-known/*  /oauth/token  /oauth/register  /mcp  /sse  /cli/*  → public (bearer/DCR)
       /oauth/authorize                                                   → Access-gated (only human step)
```

**AUD reuse:** add `mcp.yukitools.dev/oauth/authorize` as a **destination on the
existing `ctxlayer.yukitools.dev` Access app** (AUD `b0dee578…`, policy "Yukitools
Eligible"). Same app ⇒ same AUD ⇒ the Worker's existing `CF_ACCESS_AUD` validates the
Access JWT from both the browser host and the MCP authorize path. No new AUD/env.

## Resulting MCP sign-in flow
1. Client → `mcp.yukitools.dev/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` (public) → AS discovery.
2. Client DCR `/oauth/register` (public), opens `/oauth/authorize?...` in a browser.
3. Access intercepts `/oauth/authorize` → Entra login → back **with `Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion`**.
4. `handleAuthorize` verifies the Access JWT, upserts `idp='access'` user, calls
   `completeMcpAuthorization` → 302 to the client with the code.
5. Client exchanges code at `/oauth/token` (public) → bearer token (props userId/email/role).
6. Client calls `/mcp` (public, bearer) → `McpSessionDO` reads `ctx.props`. Done.

## Work items

### A. App change (one file, ~120 lines, generic — gated on existing `CF_ACCESS_*`)
- `apps/worker/src/oauth/authorize-page.ts` → `handleAuthorize(request, env)`: add a

1	/**
2	 * Nightly prune of abandoned DCR client registrations.
3	 *
4	 * MCP hosts that use RFC 8252 §7.3 loopback redirects (Claude Code,
5	 * Cursor, Windsurf, …) do a fresh Dynamic Client Registration per auth
6	 * attempt — each mints a new public `client_id` on an ephemeral
7	 * `http://localhost:<port>/callback`. Attempts that are retried,
8	 * cancelled, or superseded leave behind a registration with no grant.
9	 * `workers-oauth-provider` never expires client records, so without a
10	 * sweep these accumulate forever and clutter the admin viewer.
11	 *
12	 * Policy (see `isPrunableClient`): delete a client iff it is PUBLIC
13	 * (token_endpoint_auth_method='none'), has ZERO grants, and was
14	 * registered more than `olderThanDays` ago. Confidential clients
15	 * (stable hosted redirects, e.g. claude.ai) are never auto-pruned even
16	 * with zero grants — a missing grant there reads as "not used yet",
17	 * not "abandoned".
18	 *
19	 * Fail-closed: if the grant index is incomplete (a per-user
20	 * listUserGrants read failed, so a real grant could be invisible) we
21	 * delete NOTHING this run and report it. A legitimate client must never
22	 * be deleted because a transient KV read made it look orphaned.
23	 */
24	
25	import type { Env } from '../env'
26	import { buildUserGrantIndex, type OAuthHelpers } from './client-grants'
27	import { errMessage } from '../util/errors'
28	
29	const SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86400
30	
31	export interface PruneClientsResult {
32	  scanned: number
33	  /** Clients matching the prune policy. */
34	  orphans: number
35	  deleted: number
36	  /** deleteClient calls that threw. */
37	  failed: number
38	  /** True when we declined to delete because the grant index undercounts. */
39	  skippedIncompleteIndex: boolean
40	  deletedIds: string[]
41	}
42	
43	/** Minimal shape of a client record needed to decide prunability. */
44	interface ClientLike {
45	  clientId: string
46	  tokenEndpointAuthMethod: string
47	  registrationDate?: number | null
48	}
49	
50	/**
51	 * Pure prune predicate. `grantIndex` keys are clients that hold ≥1
52	 * grant; absence ⇒ zero grants. `cutoffSeconds` is the youngest
53	 * registration timestamp we'll still delete (older = prunable).
54	 */
55	export function isPrunableClient(
56	  client: ClientLike,
57	  grantIndex: ReadonlyMap<string, unknown>,
58	  cutoffSeconds: number
59	): boolean {
60	  if (client.tokenEndpointAuthMethod !== 'none') return false // confidential
61	  if (grantIndex.has(client.clientId)) return false // has grants
62	  // No registrationDate ⇒ can't age it ⇒ keep (don't delete blind).
63	  if (typeof client.registrationDate !== 'number') return false
64	  return client.registrationDate < cutoffSeconds
65	}
66	
67	/**
68	 * Core loop, decoupled from the grant-index build so it's unit-testable
69	 * with a mock helpers + a plain Map. Paginates all clients and deletes
70	 * the prunable ones best-effort.
71	 */
72	export async function pruneClientsByPolicy(
73	  helpers: Pick<OAuthHelpers, 'listClients' | 'deleteClient'>,
74	  grantIndex: ReadonlyMap<string, unknown>,
75	  cutoffSeconds: number
76	): Promise<Omit<PruneClientsResult, 'skippedIncompleteIndex'>> {
77	  let scanned = 0
78	  let orphans = 0
79	  let deleted = 0
80	  let failed = 0
81	  const deletedIds: string[] = []
82	
83	  let cursor: string | undefined
84	  let pages = 0
85	  do {
86	    const page = await helpers.listClients({ limit: 200, cursor })
87	    for (const client of page.items) {
88	      scanned++
89	      if (!isPrunableClient(client, grantIndex, cutoffSeconds)) continue
90	      orphans++
91	      try {
92	        await helpers.deleteClient(client.clientId)
93	        deleted++
94	        deletedIds.push(client.clientId)
95	      } catch (err) {
96	        failed++
97	        console.warn(
98	          `[prune-clients] deleteClient(${client.clientId}) failed:`,
99	          errMessage(err)
100	        )
101	      }
102	    }
103	    cursor = page.cursor
104	    // Safety backstop against an ill-behaved cursor — 50×200 = 10k
105	    // clients, far beyond any realistic registration count.
106	    if (++pages > 50) {
107	      console.warn('[prune-clients] stopped after 50 pages; cursor may be looping')
108	      break
109	    }
110	  } while (cursor)
111	
112	  return { scanned, orphans, deleted, failed, deletedIds }
113	}
114	
115	export async function pruneOrphanOAuthClients(
116	  env: Env,
117	  helpers: OAuthHelpers,
118	  opts: { olderThanDays: number; now?: number }
119	): Promise<PruneClientsResult> {
120	  const nowSeconds = opts.now ?? Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)
121	  const cutoff = nowSeconds - opts.olderThanDays * SECONDS_PER_DAY
122	
123	  const { index, complete } = await buildUserGrantIndex(env, helpers)
124	  if (!complete) {
125	    return {
126	      scanned: 0,
127	      orphans: 0,
128	      deleted: 0,
129	      failed: 0,
130	      skippedIncompleteIndex: true,
131	      deletedIds: []
132	    }
133	  }
134	
135	  const core = await pruneClientsByPolicy(helpers, index, cutoff)
136	  return { ...core, skippedIncompleteIndex: false }
137	}

1	/**
2	 * clientId → user-grant[] index, shared by the OAuth-clients admin
3	 * viewer (`api/admin-oauth-clients.ts`) and the orphan-client prune
4	 * (`oauth/prune-clients.ts`).
5	 *
6	 * The SDK has no inverse "grants for client" lookup, so we fan
7	 * `OAuthHelpers.listUserGrants` over every ctxlayer user in parallel
8	 * and group by `clientId`. A client absent from the returned map has
9	 * zero grants — which is exactly the signal both callers need (the
10	 * viewer renders "none"; the prune treats it as an abandoned
11	 * registration).
12	 *
13	 * Per-user failures are swallowed so one bad read can't fail the admin
14	 * page — but we surface a `complete` flag alongside the index. That
15	 * matters for the prune: a swallowed failure makes a user's real grants
16	 * LOOK like zero, which would make a legitimate client look orphaned.
17	 * The prune therefore refuses to delete anything when `complete` is
18	 * false (fail-closed); the viewer ignores the flag and shows the
19	 * best-effort index.
20	 *
21	 * Each (client, user) pair appears once; we keep the earliest
22	 * `createdAt` as `grantedAt` — the original authorisation moment, which
23	 * is what the admin cares about (refresh exchanges create new grant
24	 * rows over time).
25	 */
26	
27	import type { getOAuthApi } from '@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider'
28	import type { OAuthClientUserRef } from '@ctxlayer/shared'
29	import type { Env } from '../env'
30	import { listUserRefs } from '../db/queries/users'
31	import { errMessage } from '../util/errors'
32	
33	export type OAuthHelpers = ReturnType<typeof getOAuthApi<Env>>
34	
35	export interface UserGrantIndex {
36	  /** clientId → users who hold a grant on it. Absent key = zero grants. */
37	  index: Map<string, OAuthClientUserRef[]>
38	  /** False if any per-user listUserGrants read failed (index undercounts). */
39	  complete: boolean
40	}
41	
42	export async function buildUserGrantIndex(
43	  env: Env,
44	  helpers: OAuthHelpers
45	): Promise<UserGrantIndex> {
46	  const users = await listUserRefs(env)
47	  if (users.length === 0) return { index: new Map(), complete: true }
48	  const perUser = await Promise.all(
49	    users.map(async (u) => {
50	      try {
51	        // listUserGrants is paginated; we pull the first page only
52	        // since our scale is bounded. Promote to full pagination if
53	        // a single user ever accumulates >200 grants (unlikely).
54	        const page = await helpers.listUserGrants(u.id, { limit: 200 })
55	        return { user: u, grants: page.items, ok: true }
56	      } catch (err) {
57	        console.warn(
58	          `[client-grants] listUserGrants(${u.id}) failed:`,
59	          errMessage(err)
60	        )
61	        return { user: u, grants: [], ok: false }
62	      }
63	    })
64	  )
65	
66	  const complete = perUser.every((r) => r.ok)
67	  const index = new Map<string, OAuthClientUserRef[]>()
68	  for (const { user, grants } of perUser) {
69	    for (const g of grants) {
70	      const list = index.get(g.clientId) ?? []
71	      const existing = list.find((ref) => ref.userId === user.id)
72	      if (existing) {
73	        if (g.createdAt < existing.grantedAt) existing.grantedAt = g.createdAt
74	      } else {
75	        list.push({
76	          userId: user.id,
77	          email: user.email,
78	          name: user.name,
79	          grantedAt: g.createdAt
80	        })
81	      }
82	      index.set(g.clientId, list)
83	    }
84	  }
85	  // Stable ordering per client — earliest grant first.
86	  for (const list of index.values()) list.sort((a, b) => a.grantedAt - b.grantedAt)
87	  return { index, complete }
88	}

/**
 * A6 (2026-08 review): per-call credential freshness for user-scoped
 * upstream strategies.
 *
 * User credentials are decrypted and bound to the upstream client when the
 * MCP session initialises, so without this check a mid-session disconnect
 * (user removes the connection), admin wipe, or reauth-required flag would
 * keep working until the session dies. One D1 point-read per call makes
 * revocation bite within one call instead. The async job path re-resolves
 * the bearer from D1 at execution time, so the inline path was the only
 * stale window — but the guard runs before the async SUBMIT too, so a
 * revoked user can't queue new jobs either.
 *
 * Shared/none strategies are exempt: they are org-wide operator config,
 * not a per-user grant, and revocation there is an upstream-disable.
 */

import type { Env } from '../env'
import { getUserCredentialStatus } from '../db/queries/upstream-credentials'

export interface FreshnessConn {
  id: string
  slug: string
  authStrategy: string
}

/**
 * Returns the agent-facing error text when the user's credential for this
 * upstream is gone or flagged for re-auth, or null when the call may
 * proceed. First-party guidance (no upstream input), safe to surface.
 */
export async function credentialFreshnessError(
  env: Env,
  userId: string,
  conn: FreshnessConn
): Promise<string | null> {
  if (conn.authStrategy !== 'user_bearer' && conn.authStrategy !== 'user_oauth') return null
  const status = await getUserCredentialStatus(env, userId, conn.id)
  if (status.present && !status.needsReauth) return null
  const reason = status.present
    ? 'requires re-authorization (its token could not be refreshed)'
    : 'has been disconnected'
  return (
    `credential_revoked: your ${conn.slug} connection ${reason}. ` +
    `Reconnect it on the ctxlayer Upstreams page, then call reload_upstreams ` +
    `(or start a new session).`
  )
}

content.text:
The daily reconnects don't trace to a refresh-token regression in ctxlayer. Your upstreams' authorizations expire on a fixed clock that refreshing can't extend, and when one dies its tools drop out of the session with no warning. I changed nothing in code or prod; live is still `fa0ba67` from 2026-09-04. I used only read-only D1 SELECTs and OAuth KV key-name listing with the ops token. The ops token can't read Workers Logs (`Authentication error`), so I left those alone.

## Part 2: upstreams expire on a fixed clock

`created_at → reauth_required_at` in `user_credentials`, plus the 36 `upstream.reauth_required` audit rows of the last 3 weeks:

| upstream | lifetime from authorize | currently flagged | reason logged |
|---|---|---|---|
| up-datadog | 14.1–14.8 days | 14 of 22 | standard `invalid_grant` text |
| up-linear | about 25.0 days | 6 of 29 | `Grant not found` / `Refresh token has expired` |
| up-sentry | 30.0 days | 14 of 29 | `Grant not found` |
| up-survicate (added 09-14) | about 1 day | 4 of 5 | `Invalid or expired grant` |

- **Linear and Sentry:** their error strings are verbatim from `@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider`, the library ctxlayer uses. Its refresh-token lifetime is set once at authorization and never extended by a refresh, so keep-warm can't prevent these expiries.
- **Cohorts:** users connect in batches, so they expire in batches. The Linear batch from 08-20 died 09-14 to 09-17, which is the complaint week.
- **Next Linear expiry:** 7 users authorized Linear on 08-24. On the 25-day estimate they lose it tomorrow between about 09:45 and 13:45 CEST, unless they reconnect Linear at `/app/upstreams` first.
- **Survicate** is the only upstream dying daily, and it isn't a clean fixed lifetime: one credential was alive at 32h, another dead at 23h. I suspect its refresh-token rotation is breaking. I haven't investigated that.

## Part 1: Claude → ctxlayer login

- **The server side looks healthy.** Grants 3–4 weeks old are still refreshing right now, and nothing server-side is killing logins. The nightly client prune deletes at most 5 unused registrations, and grant revocation only runs on admin suspend/delete. The August library upgrade (0.7.0 → 0.10.3) didn't change the TTL defaults or the refresh logic; I compared both.
- **Re-auths are rising.** They went from about 2/day in mid-August to 10–15/day this week, and client registrations went from 219 to 408 in 19 days. The old grants of users who re-authed are still valid on the server, so ctxlayer never revoked those logins.
- **Two causes remain possible, and I can't tell them apart:**
  - Users reconnect by reflex when upstream tools vanish. The re-auth spike lines up with the Linear die-off.
  - Concurrent Claude processes race on refresh: the library accepts only the current and one previous refresh token, and access tokens last 1 hour.
- **One check settles it:** in the Cloudflare dashboard, search the `ctxlayer-yukitools` logs for `OAuth error response` over 7 days.
  - `Invalid refresh token` means the race.
  - `Grant not found` or `expired` means ctxlayer's own 30-day login expiry.
  - No hits means users are reconnecting on their own.
- Adding Workers Observability read permission to the ops token would let me run that check myself.

## Confirmed code gaps (answers to Jan's questions)

| # | gap | where |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | An upstream needing re-auth registers zero tools and nothing announces it, so the agent has no tools and may improvise. | `mcp/proxy-registry.ts`, server instructions |
| 2 | `connected: true` and `needsReauth: true` appear together, and an unconnected upstream still shows its catalogue `toolsCount`. | `mcp/catalogue-views.ts:315` |
| 3 | `reload_upstreams` reported `added: []` after a real 0 → 79 recovery. My read (not reproduced): when the session wakes it re-registers the tools before the reload handler runs, so the reload finds nothing new. The fix is to persist what the client was told, the same way the hint ledger does. | `proxy-registry.ts` `refresh()`, `session-do.ts` |
| 4 | Calls blocked for a revoked credential return before usage is recorded, so they never reach the Errors table. | `proxy-registry.ts` call handler |
| 5 | Keep-warm counts credentials that needed no refresh as "warmed". The 16 never-expiring GitHub credentials and 4 Sentry ones are re-selected every night and hold about 20 of the 25 batch slots. | `upstream/keep-warm.ts` |

Jan's "empty success" case doesn't show in the data: 14 days of proxied-call logs contain no 401 or auth-class failures. The real danger is tools going missing (gap 1), not calls failing quietly.

## What I'd build, in this order

1. Warn before expiry: learn each upstream's lifetime and show "Linear expires in 2 days" on `/app/upstreams` and in `list_upstreams`.
2. Fix gaps 1–3, keeping a dead upstream's tools listed so each call returns a hard `credential_revoked` error.
3. Fix the keep-warm batch.
4. Make ctxlayer's refresh path race-safe, only if the log check points to the race.

Tell me which of these to start on. I won't commit or deploy until you say so. The findings are saved to memory as `project_mcp_disconnects_2026-09-17.md`.

But it shows something I hadn't seen: 13,650 errors in 7 days against only 36 re-auth flags in 3 weeks. Dead credentials are being retried over and over. Let me check why.

content.text:
The screenshot confirms Part 2 (upstream expiry) and exposes a retry storm, which I've fixed in the working tree. It doesn't answer Part 1 (the Claude → ctxlayer login), because `[oauth]` is the log prefix for the upstream side only. The fix is not committed or deployed.

## What the screenshot shows

| observation | meaning |
|---|---|
| 13,650 errors in 7 days, against only 36 re-auth flags in 3 weeks | ctxlayer keeps retrying credentials it already knows are dead |
| Peak on Sep 14, about 1.2k per 2 hours | matches the day the 08-20 Linear batch expired |
| Errors come from Sentry, Datadog, Linear and Survicate, never ADO or GitHub | only upstreams that use dynamic client registration are affected |
| Blue rows: `saveTokens … expires_in=3599` | healthy refreshes are working normally |

## Cause

In `upstream/bearer.ts` the "already flagged, skip the refresh" guard existed only on the static-OAuth path (ADO, GitHub). Linear, Sentry, Datadog and Survicate use the other path, which retried the dead refresh token every time a session started or woke from idle. That produced about 2,000 failing token requests a day to third parties, all from ctxlayer's single shared client registration.

The retry made sense before the 2026-08-28 classifier change (`34f434c`), when temporary failures could also set the flag. Since then only permanent failures set it, so a retry can never recover anything.

I also found, from reading `upstream/oauth-refresh.ts`, that when two sessions of the same user refresh at once, the one that loses the single-flight lock waits 2 seconds. It then carries on with the stored, already-expired access token. It registers that upstream's tools against a token that no longer works. This is a code path for the "everything looks connected but calls fail" case Jan described. The guard removes it for flagged credentials.

## Fix (working tree only)

- **`apps/worker/src/upstream/bearer.ts`:** I moved the existing flagged-credential guard above the branch so both paths share it. It reuses the same check, so there is no new logic.
- **`apps/worker/test/integration/oauth-static-reauth.test.ts`:** I added a test for the Linear/Sentry-style path. It fails on the old code (2 outbound calls for a dead credential) and passes on the fix.
- **`bun run verify`:** passes with 667 worker unit tests, 46 web tests and 478 integration tests. The 2 lint warnings are not in the files I changed.

After deploy, the `[oauth] … auth() threw` volume should fall from about 2,000 a day to roughly one per credential per expiry. Nothing else changes for users. A flagged credential still needs the user to reconnect, and reconnecting clears the flag.

## Still open: Part 1

Run the same log view with the search text `OAuth error response` over the last 7 days. That is ctxlayer's own OAuth server logging why it rejected a Claude client.

| what shows up | meaning |
|---|---|
| `invalid_grant - Invalid refresh token` | concurrent Claude processes racing on refresh |
| `Grant not found` or `Refresh token has expired` | ctxlayer's own 30-day login expiry |
| `invalid_client` | the Claude client's registration expired |
| almost nothing | users are reconnecting by reflex when upstream tools vanish |

The 7 users who authorized Linear on 08-24 are still due to lose it tomorrow between about 09:45 and 13:45 CEST. Asking them to reconnect Linear at `/app/upstreams` in the morning avoids a repeat of Monday.

Say the word if you want this committed. The warn-before-expiry work and the three status/reload gaps from Jan's note are separate follow-ups.

ctxlayer's own login is not failing. In that 24-hour window, 8 users re-authorized with ctxlayer, and ctxlayer had rejected at most one of them first.

## What the 5 log lines say

| line | count | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `invalid_grant - Invalid refresh token` | 0 | no refresh race; my theory was wrong |
| `invalid_client` | 0 | no expired or pruned client registrations |
| `invalid_grant - Grant not found` | 2 | the login no longer exists on the server |
| `invalid_token - Invalid access token` | 3 | two are the retry straight after the lines above, one is a stray |

Both `Grant not found` rejections are exact 30-day expiries. `oauth/provider-config.ts` doesn't set `refreshTokenTTL`, so the library default applies: a hard 30 days from login, never extended by use.

| client registered (UTC) | refresh rejected (UTC) |
|---|---|
| 08-18 07:34 | 09-17 08:41, the first hourly refresh after 30 days |
| 08-18 13:17 | 09-17 13:24 |

With about 50 users on several clients each, that gives a steady 2 forced re-logins a day, which is the configured behaviour, not something that broke.

#   scripts/release-all.sh dev stage          # only these hosts

set -euo pipefail

OPS_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
APP_REPO="${APP_REPO:-$(cd "$OPS_ROOT/../ctxlayer" 2>/dev/null && pwd || true)}"
[[ -n "$APP_REPO" && -f "$APP_REPO/wrangler.toml" ]] || {
  echo "✗ APP_REPO not found (sibling ../ctxlayer). Set APP_REPO=/path/to/ctxlayer." >&2

}
TEMPLATE="$OPS_ROOT/wrangler.template.toml"
REGISTRY="$OPS_ROOT/tenants.json"
[ -s "$REGISTRY" ] || { echo "✗ no tenant registry at $REGISTRY." >&2; exit 1; }

# Preflight: fail fast on deploy-scheme naming drift (binding/cron parity) so a
# templated tenant can't silently lose a binding or a queue/cron consumer.
APP_REPO="$APP_REPO" "$OPS_ROOT/scripts/check-deploy-scheme.sh"

MIGRATE_ONLY=0
SELECTED=()
for a in "$@"; do
  if [[ "$a" == "--migrate-only" ]]; then MIGRATE_ONLY=1; else SELECTED+=("$a"); fi
done
if [[ ${#SELECTED[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then
  # No `mapfile`/`readarray` — macOS ships bash 3.2, where they don't exist.
  while IFS= read -r slug; do SELECTED+=("$slug"); done < <(jq -r 'keys[]' "$REGISTRY")
fi
[[ ${#SELECTED[@]} -gt 0 ]] || { echo "✗ nothing to release." >&2; exit 1; }

# Cross-account guard (see docs/yukitools-provisioning.md): keep only the

  fi

  echo "── $SLUG ($HOST)${MCP_HOST:+ +$MCP_HOST}${CF_ACCESS_TEAM:+ [access]} ──"
  WORKER="$WORKER" HOST="$HOST" D1_ID="$D1_ID" KV_ID="$KV_ID" \
  ALLOWED_GOOGLE_HD="$GOOGLE_HD" ALLOWED_GOOGLE_EMAILS="$GOOGLE_EMAILS" \
  ALLOWED_GITHUB_ORG="$GITHUB_ORG" ALLOWED_GITHUB_USERS="$GITHUB_USERS" \
  CF_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN="$CF_ACCESS_TEAM" CF_ACCESS_AUD="$CF_ACCESS_AUD" \
  MCP_ROUTE_BLOCK="$MCP_ROUTE_BLOCK" MCP_PUBLIC_URL="$MCP_PUBLIC_URL" \
  GATEWAY_ALIAS="$GATEWAY_ALIAS" \
    envsubst '${WORKER} ${HOST} ${D1_ID} ${KV_ID} ${ALLOWED_GOOGLE_HD} ${ALLOWED_GOOGLE_EMAILS} ${ALLOWED_GITHUB_ORG} ${ALLOWED_GITHUB_USERS} ${CF_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN} ${CF_ACCESS_AUD} ${MCP_ROUTE_BLOCK} ${MCP_PUBLIC_URL} ${GATEWAY_ALIAS}' \
    < "$TEMPLATE" > "$APP_REPO/$CFG"

    # JSON body — treat 200 (open / bypass) or 302 (Access enforcing) as healthy.
    code=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://${HOST}/api/health" || true)

  fi
done

/**

 * `@cloudflare/workers-oauth-provider` — PKCE enforcement, redirect_uri
 * matching, authorization-code single-use. The 2026-07 review flagged them
 * as delegated-and-unverifiable (the library is not vendored, so nothing
 * in-repo asserted them). These tests run the real provider against real
 * KV in workerd, so a library upgrade that regresses any of them fails CI

 * The flow mirrors production exactly: clients register through the real
 * /oauth/register endpoint, the authorize leg uses the same

const BASE = 'https://ctxlayer-oauth-sec.test'
const REDIRECT = 'https://client.example/callback'
const OTHER_REDIRECT = 'https://evil.example/steal'

// Stub default handler: these tests only exercise the provider's own
// endpoints, so the fallthrough should never be reached.
const provider = new OAuthProvider<WorkerEnv>(
  oauthProviderOptions({
    fetch: () => Promise.resolve(new Response('unexpected fallthrough', { status: 500 }))
  })
)

async function pfetch(input: string, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {
  const ctx = createExecutionContext()
  const res = await provider.fetch(new Request(input, init), testEnv, ctx)
  await waitOnExecutionContext(ctx)
  return res
}

async function registerPublicClient(): Promise<string> {
  const res = await pfetch(`${BASE}/oauth/register`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' },

      redirect_uris: [REDIRECT],
      token_endpoint_auth_method: 'none',
      grant_types: ['authorization_code', 'refresh_token'],
      response_types: ['code']
    })
  })
  expect(res.status).toBe(201)
  const body = (await res.json()) as { client_id: string }
  return body.client_id
}

/**
 * How long an MCP client's login lasts before the user must re-authorize.
 * The library stamps this ONCE at the authorization-code exchange and never
 * slides it on refresh — it is an absolute lifetime, not an idle timeout. The
 * library default (30 days) forced every client of every user through a
 * monthly re-login for no security gain: suspend/delete already revoke all
 * of a user's grants instantly (oauth/revoke-grants.ts) and the session DO

 * registration lifetime (`clientRegistrationTTL` default), which caps a

 * refresh into `invalid_client` instead of `invalid_grant`; both mean
 * "log in again". Applies to NEW logins only: existing grants keep the
 * expiry they were issued with.
 */
export const MCP_LOGIN_TTL_SECONDS = 90 * 24 * 60 * 60

-- When the CURRENT upstream grant was issued — i.e. the last interactive
-- authorization (OAuth code exchange), not the last token refresh.
--
-- Several upstream MCP servers give a grant a fixed ABSOLUTE lifetime from
-- the moment of authorization that no amount of refreshing extends (field
-- finding 2026-09-17: Datadog 14d, Linear ~25d, Sentry 30d). With this
-- stamp plus the admin-configured `authConfig.grantLifetimeDays`, ctxlayer
-- can warn BEFORE the cliff instead of discovering the death at the next
-- refresh. `created_at` can't carry this: the upsert keeps it across a
-- re-authorization that reuses the row, and `updated_at` moves on every
-- refresh.
--
-- Backfill from `created_at`: until now every interactive re-auth went
-- through a DELETE + INSERT of the row (Disconnect, or the wipe-and-retry
-- in api/upstream-oauth.ts), so for existing rows the two coincide.
-- Additive nullable column on a child table — no rebuild (G1 not in play).
ALTER TABLE user_credentials ADD COLUMN granted_at INTEGER;
UPDATE user_credentials SET granted_at = created_at WHERE granted_at IS NULL;

/**
 * Generic, pluggable upstream-client abstraction. Each transport family is
 * one implementation behind this interface; `createUpstreamClient` (in
 * `create-client.ts`) is the single dispatch point, so a future transport
 * slots in without re-plumbing the proxy/dispatch layer in
 * `mcp/tools-proxy.ts`.
 *
 * This module is the canonical home for the catalogue/result shapes and
 * the dialable-transport predicate. It imports nothing from the rest of
 * the worker — implementations depend on it, never the other way around.
 */

import type { SupportedTransport } from '@ctxlayer/shared'

export interface UpstreamCatalogueTool {
  toolName: string
  description: string | null
  inputSchema: unknown
}

export interface UpstreamCallResult {
  content: unknown
  isError?: boolean
  structuredContent?: unknown
}

export interface UpstreamClient {
  listTools(): Promise<UpstreamCatalogueTool[]>
  callTool(name: string, args: unknown): Promise<UpstreamCallResult>
  close(): Promise<void>
}

/**
 * The transports the worker can actually dial over HTTP. Any other
 * transport value (a legacy or forged DB row) must never surface as a
 * dialable connection. Single source of truth — SQL IN lists and
 * row-filtering checks are both built from this tuple.
 */
export const DIALABLE_TRANSPORTS = ['streamable_http', 'sse'] as const

input.content:
-- Nightly keep-warm scheduling, decoupled from `updated_at`.
--
-- The job selected "oauth credentials whose `updated_at` is ≥14 days old",
-- oldest first, 25 per night — relying on a successful warm to re-save the
-- tokens and so move `updated_at` out of the window. But most attempts save
-- nothing: a token with no expiry and no refresh token (GitHub OAuth apps)
-- or one whose access token is still valid (Sentry) resolves without a
-- refresh. Those credentials stayed due FOREVER, were re-selected every
-- night, and — being the oldest — permanently held the front of the batch
-- (2026-09 yukitools: the same ~20 credentials "warmed" nightly for weeks,
-- 20 of 25 slots; any growth past 25 would have starved the credentials the
-- job exists for).
--
-- `keep_warm_after` = do not consider this credential again before this unix
-- time. Every attempt stamps it (a full idle window ahead when there was
-- nothing to do or the refresh worked; ~a day ahead after a transient
-- failure), and the due query orders by it, so an attempted credential
-- always moves to the back of the queue. NULL = never attempted.
-- Additive nullable column on a child table — no rebuild (G1 not in play).
ALTER TABLE user_credentials ADD COLUMN keep_warm_after INTEGER;

369:export async function listKeepWarmDueCredentials(
 * user_oauth credentials due for the nightly keep-warm refresh
 * (upstream/keep-warm.ts): oauth-kind, not flagged for reauth, on an
 * enabled upstream, and untouched for at least `idleSeconds` —
 * `updated_at` moves on every token save, so normal session traffic
 * naturally exempts active credentials. Oldest first, capped at `limit`
 * per run to bound refresh-token rotation spend.
 */
export async function listKeepWarmDueCredentials(
  env: Env,
  nowSec: number,
  idleSeconds: number,
  limit: number
): Promise<Array<{ userId: string; upstream: UpstreamServerRow }>> {
  const res = await env.DB.prepare(
    `SELECT uc.user_id AS cred_user_id, us.*
     FROM user_credentials uc
     JOIN upstream_servers us ON us.id = uc.upstream_id
     WHERE uc.kind = 'oauth'
       AND uc.reauth_required_at IS NULL
       AND us.enabled = 1
       AND uc.updated_at <= ?1 - ?2
     ORDER BY uc.updated_at ASC
     LIMIT ?3`
  )
    .bind(nowSec, idleSeconds, limit)
    .all<UpstreamServerRow & { cred_user_id: string }>()
  return (res.results ?? []).map(({ cred_user_id, ...upstream }) => ({
    userId: cred_user_id,
    upstream: upstream as UpstreamServerRow
  }))
}

content.text:
The keep-warm job is fixed in the working tree, uncommitted and undeployed like the rest of today's batch. Full `bun run verify` passes (677 worker unit, 51 web, 494 integration tests); nothing has run against prod.

## What was wrong

The job decided who was "due" from `updated_at` and relied on a successful warm re-saving the tokens to push a credential out of the 14-day window. Most attempts save nothing, so those credentials stayed due forever. They are the oldest, so they sat at the front of the 25-slot batch every night and were tallied as `warmed`:

| credentials | why nothing was saved |
|---|---|
| 16 × up-github | The token has no expiry and no refresh token, so there is nothing to refresh. |
| 4 × up-sentry | Inferred, since I can't decrypt tokens: the access token is still valid after 14 idle days, so no refresh is attempted. |

That is 20 of 25 slots. Once more than 25 credentials were due, the ones the job exists for would never have been reached.

Every `failed: 1` in the ledger since 08-29 lines up with a re-auth flag written at 03:00 that night. Those were dead authorizations being detected, which is the job working, yet they turned the run yellow.

## The fix

- **Own schedule.** Migration 0037 adds `keep_warm_after` to each credential. Every attempt stamps when to look again, and the due query orders by that stamp, so an attempted credential goes to the back of the queue.
- **When to look again.** After a refresh or when there was nothing to do, the stamp is 14 days ahead. After a transient failure it is 20 hours ahead. It is 20 rather than 24 because the stamp is taken from the cron's scheduled time, and 24 hours would land just after the next night's run.
- **Honest counts.** The job now reads what actually happened off the credential row. The run summary has `refreshed`, `flagged`, `failed`, `idle` (nothing to refresh) and `backlog` (due but not reached). `refreshed` means a token was really renewed, `flagged` means a dead authorization was detected, and `failed` is now transient failures only.
- **Status.** A run is `partial` only when something actually failed. A detected death keeps it `ok`.
- The Jobs dashboard renders summaries generically, so the new counters appear without front-end work.

## How I checked it

Putting the old selection rule back makes exactly the 4 new scheduling tests fail, including a 25-credential starvation scenario and a test that a nothing-to-do credential isn't due again the next night. With the fix restored, all 11 keep-warm tests pass.

## What to expect after deploy

The first night should show roughly `idle: 20, backlog: 0`, as each stuck credential gets its one attempt and is stamped. After that `due` should sit near zero, with occasional `flagged` entries on green runs.

I did not make the job force a refresh when the access token is still valid. That would spend rotating refresh tokens, which goes against the un-aggressive design you chose, and for Sentry the authorization ends at 30 days whatever the job does.

Three things are now waiting for your "commit": the 90-day login, the dead-upstream work with the expiry warning, and this. `upstream-credentials.ts` carries changes from both of the last two, so I saved the earlier diff and can still split them into separate commits. The deploy command from before now applies migrations 0036 and 0037.

git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(upstream): dead upstream authorizations are loud, predictable and renewable

Upstream MCP authorizations die on the PROVIDER's clock: several give a
grant a fixed absolute lifetime from the moment the user authorized, which
no amount of refreshing extends (field finding 2026-09-17: Datadog 14d,
Linear ~25d, Sentry 30d — the latter two run workers-oauth-provider, whose
refresh-token TTL is stamped once at the code exchange). ctxlayer handled
the death silently: the session registered NONE of the upstream's tools,
list_upstreams said `connected: true, needsReauth: true`, the Upstreams
page showed a green "connected", and reload_upstreams answered "Nothing
new" after a real 0 → 79 recovery. Agents with no tools improvise; users
reconnected the MCP connector every morning, which fixes nothing.

Loud
- proxy-registry: an upstream whose credential is on file but yields no
  bearer (flagged, or a refresh that failed just now) is LISTED from the
  cached catalogue with no client bound. Calls fail with first-party
  `credential_revoked` text naming the absolute Upstreams URL.
- The freshness gate runs inside the handler's try, so blocked calls are
  RECORDED (new usage code `credential_revoked`) — they used to return
  before any usage row, hiding exactly the users who needed help.
- `ensureBound`: bind on demand, and REBIND when the stored credential
  changed since the client was bound (`updated_at` stamp). A retry after
  re-authorizing just works — no reload_upstreams, no connector reconnect
  — and a live session no longer calls on with a superseded token.
- list_upstreams: one `status` (ready | needs_reauth | not_connected);
  `connected` is true only when ready; `toolsCount` = callable now, with
  the catalogue size in `availableTools`. CONTRACT CHANGE for readers of
  the old fields.
- reload_upstreams reports added / recovered / still-unusable upstreams
  and always emits tools/list_changed (a DO wake re-runs init, so the diff
  against the new instance was empty exactly when people call it).
- /api/upstreams gains `needsReauth` + `authExpiresAt`; the Upstreams page
  renders re-authorize / expiring / connected from one `upstreamHealth`.

Predictable + renewable
- Migration 0036 `user_credentials.granted_at`: restamped ONLY by the
  callback's code exchange; a refresh keeps it (same grant upstream).
- `authConfig.grantLifetimeDays` (admin drawer) + shared `grantExpiry()`:
  expiry date on the page, a warning in list_upstreams for the last 3 days.
- `oauth/start?renew=1`: a plain Reconnect of a healthy credential only
  refreshes, which does NOT restart the provider's clock. Renew hides the
  stored tokens from the SDK for that one run so it goes interactive, and
  leaves the working credential intact until the new one lands.

Found on the way
- Saving the admin drawer on a connected DCR upstream WIPED its
  `oauth.client_info`: the read path redacts it and PATCH replaces the
  whole auth_config column, so the next auth() re-registered under a new

  user_oauth, the URL changes, or a static client takes over.
- Removes `listUserCredentialedUpstreamIds`, superseded by the status read.

## What

The "credential already flagged for reauth → skip the refresh" guard in `resolveUserUpstreamBearer` only covered the **static** OAuth path. DCR upstreams re-ran the SDK `auth()` refresh on **every** resolution — and session DOs re-run `init()` on each hibernation wake.

Field finding (2026-09-17): ~40 flagged credentials produced ~2k failing token requests/day against third-party token endpoints — 13,650 `[oauth] …: auth() threw` errors in 7 days, versus 36 actual reauth flags in 3 weeks.

## Why it was there

A leftover from before 34f434c, when transient failures also set the flag and a retry could self-heal. Only **permanent** failures flag now, so a retry can never recover anything. It also let a refresh-lease *loser* fall through to the stored, expired access token and register the upstream's tools on a dead bearer.

## Change

Hoist the guard above the static/DCR branch so both paths share it. The flag still clears on reconnect (`saveTokens → clearReauthRequired`).

## Testing

- New integration test for the DCR path — verified **red on the old code** (2 outbound calls for a credential already known dead), green with the fix.
- `bun run verify` green.

## Stack

1. **this PR** → `main`
2. #PR2 90-day MCP logins
3. #PR3 loud / predictable / renewable upstream authorizations

## Problem

Upstream MCP authorizations die on the **provider's** clock. Several give a grant a fixed absolute lifetime from the moment the user authorized, which no amount of refreshing extends (observed 2026-09: Datadog 14d, Linear ~25d, Sentry 30d — the latter two run `workers-oauth-provider`, whose refresh-token TTL is stamped once at the code exchange).

ctxlayer handled that death silently:

- the session registered **none** of the upstream's tools — an agent with no tools improvises instead of reporting a failure;
- `list_upstreams` said `connected: true, needsReauth: true`;
- the Upstreams page showed a green "connected";
- `reload_upstreams` answered "Nothing new" after a real 0 → 79 tool recovery.

Users responded by reconnecting the MCP connector every morning, which fixes nothing.

## Loud

- **proxy-registry** — an upstream whose credential is on file but yields no bearer is *listed* from the cached catalogue with no client bound; calls fail with first-party `credential_revoked` text naming the absolute Upstreams URL.
- The freshness gate now runs inside the handler's `try`, so blocked calls are **recorded** (new usage code `credential_revoked`) — they used to return before any usage row was staged.
- `ensureBound` — bind on demand, and **rebind** when the stored credential changed since the client was bound. A retry after re-authorizing just works (no `reload_upstreams`, no connector reconnect), and a live session no longer calls on with a superseded token.
- `reload_upstreams` reports added / recovered / still-unusable upstreams and always emits `tools/list_changed`.
- `/api/upstreams` gains `needsReauth` + `authExpiresAt`; the page renders re-authorize / expiring / connected from one `upstreamHealth()`.

### ⚠️ Contract change — `list_upstreams`

One `status` field (`ready | needs_reauth | not_connected`). `connected` is now true **only** when ready (it used to mean "a credential row exists"). `toolsCount` = tools callable *now* (0 unless ready); the catalogue size moves to `availableTools`. New optional `authExpiresAt` / `authExpiresInDays`.

## Predictable + renewable

- **Migration 0036** `user_credentials.granted_at` — restamped only by the callback's code exchange; a refresh keeps it. Backfilled from `created_at`.
- `authConfig.grantLifetimeDays` (admin drawer, user_oauth only) + shared pure `grantExpiry()` → expiry date on the page, and a warning in `list_upstreams` during the last 3 days.
- `oauth/start?renew=1` — a plain *Reconnect* of a healthy credential only refreshes, which does **not** restart the provider's clock. Renew hides the stored tokens from the SDK for that one run so it goes interactive, and leaves the working credential intact until the new one lands.

## Found on the way — admin edit wiped DCR client registration

Saving the admin drawer on a connected DCR upstream dropped `oauth.client_info`: the read path redacts it and PATCH replaces the whole `auth_config` column. The next `auth()` would re-register under a new `client_id`, and every user's refresh would then fail as "issued to another client". ## Problem

The nightly keep-warm selected "oauth credentials whose `updated_at` is ≥14 days old", oldest first, 25 per night — relying on a successful warm **re-saving the tokens** to move `updated_at` out of that window.

Most attempts save nothing:

| credential | why nothing is saved |
|---|---|
| no expiry + no refresh token (GitHub OAuth apps) | static path takes the refresh lease, finds nothing to refresh |
| access token still valid after two idle weeks | fast path — no refresh attempted |

Those credentials stayed due **forever**, were re-selected every night at the front of the oldest-first batch, and were tallied as `warmed`. Field finding (2026-09): the same ~20 credentials every night for weeks — 20 of 25 slots. Past 25 due, the credentials the job exists for would never have been reached.

Separately, every historical `failed: 1` in the run ledger was a death **detected** (it lines up 1:1 with a reauth flag written at 03:00 that night) — the job doing its job, shown as a yellow `partial` run.

## Change

- **Migration 0037** `user_credentials.keep_warm_after` — the job's own "don't look again before" stamp. Due = idle ≥14d **and** the stamp has passed, ordered least-recently-attempted first, so an attempted credential always moves to the back of the queue.
- Every attempt stamps it: a full idle window ahead when tokens were refreshed or there was nothing to do; **20h** after a transient failure (not 24h — the stamp is taken from the cron's scheduled time, so a full day would land just after tomorrow's run).
- Outcomes are read off the credential row instead of inferred from a non-null token: `refreshed`, `flagged`, `idle`, `failed`, plus `backlog` (due but not reached).
- A run is `partial` only on a transient failure.

Deliberately still never forces a refresh the lazy path would not make — that would spend rotating refresh tokens for no gain.

## Testing

- 6 new integration tests incl. a batch-sized starvation scenario and "a nothing-to-do credential is not due again the next night".
- **Mutation-checked:** restoring the old selection rule fails exactly the 4 new scheduling tests.
- `bun run verify` green.

## Deploy

Applies migration 0037. Expected signature: first night ≈ `idle: 20, backlog: 0` (each stuck credential gets its one attempt and is stamped), then `due` near zero.

    feat(auth): session epoch (A7) + per-call credential freshness (A6) — phase 4.4
    
    A7 — the SPA session cookie was a stateless 30-day HMAC bearer with no
    server-side kill switch: sign-out only cleared the browser's copy.
    Migration 0033 adds users.session_epoch; the cookie embeds the epoch it
    was minted under and the per-request user fetch in auth/middleware
    rejects a mismatch (401 + cookie clear). Sign-out and admin suspend bump
    the epoch, killing every outstanding cookie at once. Pre-deploy cookies
    normalise to epoch 0 — nobody is force-logged-out by the deploy; their
    next sign-out invalidates for real.
    
    A6 — user-scoped upstream creds are decrypted and bound to the client at
    MCP session init, so a mid-session disconnect / admin wipe / reauth flag
    stayed usable until the session died. mcp/credential-freshness.ts adds a
    one-point-read-per-call gate in the proxy handler (user_bearer/user_oauth
    only; runs before the async submit too). The async EXECUTION path already
    re-resolves the bearer from D1 per job. Blocked calls get first-party
    reconnect guidance (credential_revoked).
    
    Tests: session epoch unit round-trip incl. legacy-cookie normalisation;
    integration end-to-end via /api/me (accept → bump → reject → fresh cookie
    works); A6 gate against real D1 (healthy / reauth-flagged / deleted /
    shared-strategy exemption).
